questions.question: In what order does NeRF process a single pixel?
options: MLP → Ray March → Volume Render → Camera
Camera → Coordinates → Ray March → PE → MLP → Volume Render
Volume Render → MLP → Ray March → Camera
Ray March → Camera → MLP → PE → Volume Render
questions.explanation: The pipeline flows: Camera math (pixel→ray) → Coordinate transform (cam→world) → Ray marching (sample points) → Positional Encoding (project to high-D) → MLP (predict σ, color) → Volume rendering (blend to final pixel).

questions.question: Why does training NeRF from multiple camera views force the network to learn true 3D structure?
options: Because multi-view consistency — the only way to produce correct colors from ALL angles is to learn the true 3D arrangement
Because each camera adds more parameters to the network
Because more cameras means more pixels to overfit to
questions.explanation: If the network 'cheated' by pasting a flat image at one camera, it would produce wrong colors from other cameras, increasing the loss. The multi-view constraint forces the network to find the 3D structure that consistently explains ALL training views.

questions.question: What is the main computational bottleneck of NeRF?
options: Querying the MLP tens of millions of times per image (each query requires matrix multiplications through 8 layers)
questions.explanation: For an 800×800 image with 128 samples per ray, NeRF must evaluate the MLP 82 million times. Each evaluation involves 8 layers of 256×256 matrix multiplications. This is ~50 billion FLOPs per frame — the reason modern methods like Instant-NGP and 3D Gaussian Splatting exist.
